10436-erick-and-sally:
Johanna Spyri, author of Heidi, wrote this Swiss children's story, translated by Helene H. Boll in 1921. Erick and Sally live in Upper Wood, where a parsonage school, a village call, and a lost hymn shape their days. The tone is gentle, moral, and full of mountain light.

Lizebeth on the warpath, disturbance in school and home, Organ-Sunday, and a secret kept carry the plot, with surprising things happening at last. Erick enlists in a fighting army of children, in Spyri's kindly sense. Readers get a warm, old-style Swiss tale of friendship, faith, and growing up.
10800-the-anatomy-of-melancholy:
Robert Burton, writing as Democritus Junior, published The Anatomy of Melancholy in 1621, a vast study of sadness in all its kinds. This edition re-edits a modernized nineteenth-century text against the 1638 edition, correcting errors in spelling, names, and Latin. Burton divides melancholy by causes, symptoms, and cures, in long, learned partitions.

The book mixes medicine, philosophy, theology, and wit, quoting ancients and moderns on every page. Its famous preface and digressions range far beyond sickness itself. Readers get a masterpiece of English prose, endlessly quotable, on the mind's oldest affliction.
10936-the-girl-aviators-motor-butterfly:
Margaret Burnham sent her girl aviators on a cross-country flight in this 1912 adventure for young readers. Peggy Prescott, Jess Bancroft, and Bess Marshall plan a tour by air, calling their machines motor butterflies, with the Golden Butterfly and the Red Dragon leading the way. Boys Roy and Jimsy join the party, and Aunt Sally Prescott chaperones.

Storms, gypsies, a lost child called Wren, moonshiners, and a mid-air race keep the trip eventful, and Peggy's quick thinking saves a farm and settles a contest. The story celebrates pluck, friendship, and early flying, when aeroplanes were still a novelty. It belongs to a series that gave girls the same daring air adventures boys were already getting.
11970-wife-in-name-only:
Charlotte M. Braeme, writing as Bertha M. Clay, was a prolific author of sensation fiction, and Wife in Name Only belongs to that popular world, alongside Dora Thorne, From Gloom to Sunlight, Her Martyrdom, and Lady Damer's Secret. The Chicago edition lists her uniform-style titles, a sign of a readership that bought her novels in sets.

Within the story, a heroine has refused brilliant offers of marriage, including an Italian Prince Cetti who would give his possessions to take her to his sunny land. Another woman warns Lord Arleigh against a girl she once kept carefully out of his sight. Marriage, reputation, and refused suitors drive a plot built for readers who liked strong feeling and moral complication.
1207-nada-the-lily:
H. Rider Haggard sets this Zulu novel in the days of Chaka, the great king, and follows Umslopogaas, the mighty warrior, and Nada, the beautiful lily, whose love defies kings and witchdoctors. The tale runs through battles, betrayals, and a tragic fate, told by the Zulu storyteller Mopo.

Haggard writes Africa with the sweep of saga, and his Zulu world is vivid, violent, and proud. The novel is darker than King Solomon's Mines, and its ending is mournful. It stands as a classic of imperial romance, best read with eyes open to its age.
12179-vandemark-s-folly:
Herbert Quick published Vandemark Folly in 1922, a novel of Iowa pioneer life told by its hero, a Dutch farmer son. The hero calls himself a flat Dutch turnip at the start, and the chapters follow his climb from farm boy to teacher, sailor, and seeker.

Vandemark learns and teaches, suffers a great loss, finds a clue at sea, and becomes Cow Vandemark on the old ridge road. Later chapters bring a grove of destiny, a plow wedding the sod, banditry, a saved treasure, and a folly named Hell Slew. Quick writes with humor and affection for prairie people, mixing tall tales with hard work. The novel stands as a late, generous chronicle of the Midwest settlement generation.
12234-mr-scarborough-s-family:
Anthony Trollope published Mr. Scarborough Family in 1883, late in his career as the chronicler of Victorian money, law, and marriage. The novel opens with Trollope promise to go back more than once, explaining events that led to the story.

Mr. Scarborough, a landowner with a disputed will, schemes to keep his estate from creditors and kin, while his sons, daughters, and lawyers tangle over marriage settlements and debts. A mid-book thread follows Dolly and a proposal to divide a business equally on marriage, with a genteel house across the water. Trollope treats greed and respectability with dry humor. The novel is a late Trollope study of how families fight over property.
12561-a-visit-to-the-holy-land-egypt-and:
Madame Ida Pfeiffer's Visit to the Holy Land, Egypt, and Italy, translated from German by H. W. Dulcken, follows a pioneering woman traveller from Vienna down the Danube. Chapter one runs from departure, a steamer scene, Hainburg, Presburg, Pesth and Ofen, through Mohacs, Peterwardein, Semlin, Belgrade, the Iron Gate and Callafat, with discomfort and bad management aboard.

Later chapters reach the Black Sea, storm and sea-sickness, Jerusalem, Nazareth and Egypt, illustrated by frontispieces of Jerusalem and Nazareth. Pfeiffer writes plainly, observantly and independently. The book is a classic of women's travel, valuable for its route, its hardships and its unsentimental eye.
13327-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch marks fifty years with this jubilee number of July 18, 1891. Mr. Punch himself looks back over one hundred volumes, from the first number of July 1841 to a table of writers, artists, and editors who made the paper. He recalls genial comrades, bright wits, and famous names gathered round the jolly old tree.

The issue also records editors lost along the way, including Tom Taylor and his long Essence of Parliament, and Horace Mayhew. Jokes, verse, and reminiscence fill the pages, but the point is history: a comic weekly pausing to tell its own story. It shows how satire, Parliament, and London life had changed together since 1841.
13337-milly-and-olly:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's Milly and Olly, new revised edition of 1914, illustrated by Ruth M. Hallock, revives a child's story written twenty-seven years earlier under the spell of Rotha and Fairfield. Two funny fair-haired children plan a journey north to Ravensnest, with Aunt Emma's picnic, wet days, a story-telling game, and Milly's birthday. Ward writes gently for young readers.

At Ravensnest, tall mountains shut the children in like a wall, while tiny wild strawberries show scarlet balls on the banks. Later, Aunt Emma teases Olly with a bag that squeaks, warning him not to stand too near, then clicks the fastening and out jumps a great green speckled frog. The book is a warm, old-fashioned holiday tale.
13624-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-1-of-6-:
A slice of Holinshed's Chronicles, volume one, book two of the history of England, tells of Brute and his descent. Brute slew his father in hunting, was banished, wrote to King Pandrasus, fought him, took him prisoner, and made peace on conditions. Some hold Brute first peopled the island with Trojans, giants excepted, whom he utterly destroyed.

Other passages describe Indians who set precious stones in hollow places in flesh, forehead, and cheeks, like Agathyrsi painting. Brute sailed to Gaul, now France, with a great army, subdued the Gauls, returned with riches and triumph, ruled Britain nobly for forty years, and was buried at York. The slice preserves Tudor chronicle history in its own spelling.
13670-the-happy-family:
B. M. Bower, writing as B. M. Sinclair, set these linked stories among cowboys of the American West. The Happy Family is a ranch crew known for tall tales, pranks, and loyal quarrels. Each story centres on one member, often the camp liar, called the Ananias of the cow camp. Horses, cattle work, and desert travel frame the humour.

Bower knew ranch life from the inside and wrote its speech with ease. Jokes turn on bragging, mistaken identity, and practical jokes that go too far. Beneath the fun, the stories honour hard work and friendship among men far from town. The volume appeared in 1910 after magazine publication. It offers a lively, good-humoured view of the working West.
1384-the-ayrshire-legatees-or-the-pringl:
Told in letters home, this comic novel follows Dr Pringle of Ayrshire, who learns on New Year's Day that his cousin in India has left him his heir. The Pringle family sails for London to claim the fortune, and their letters report, with innocent wonder, the sights, swindles, and snobberies of the capital.

Each letter adds a fresh muddle: a wrong hotel, a bold sharper, a fashionable folly. The humour lies in the gap between Scottish thrift and London show. Written in the early nineteenth century, it is a lively epistolary comedy of a provincial family loose in a great city.
14119-the-white-riband-or-a-young-female:
F. Tennyson Jesse's 1921 novel follows Loveday, an onion-seller's daughter in a small village, as she first feels herself a woman and then a girl. Poor and watchful, she cannot afford the daydreams of a young lady. Forgetting the milk would bring no romance, only an aunt's scolding, so she carries bread and soaked pilchards home while her mind runs far ahead.

Ambition drives the plot. Loveday chases a small sum, tenpence, and a place beyond her station, braving kitchens, vicarage gates, and village gossip. Maids titter, Mrs. Veale lectures, and the Lear family watches every step. Jesse writes with sympathy and sharp comedy, showing how class draws its lines in tiny slights. The white riband of the title marks a girl's wish to be seen as more than her errands.
14396-his-family:
Ernest Poole's 1917 novel follows Roger Gale, a New York widower in his sixties, as he tries to hold his grown family together. His daughters marry, quarrel, and move into new lives, while the city around them changes.

Gale walks a New York of crowded theaters, immigrant neighborhoods, and restless youth, watching his authority fade and his affection deepen. Poole, who won the Pulitzer Prize for this book, writes plainly about aging, parenthood, and the gap between generations. The novel endures as a humane portrait of a father learning to let go.
14977-the-red-record-tabulated-statistic:
Ida B. Wells-Barnett's 1895 pamphlet The Red Record sets out tabulated statistics and alleged causes of lynching in the United States, chapter by chapter across ten chapters. A letter from Frederick Douglass opens it, thanking Wells for a faithful paper on the lynch abomination now generally practised against coloured people in the South.

Douglass writes that no word equal to it in convincing power has appeared, and that he has spoken but must now yield to her evidence. Wells-Barnett counts cases, names places and tests excuses offered for murder, showing a pattern of terror rather than justice. The pamphlet remains a core document of American investigative journalism and civil rights history.
15187-the-children-of-the-king-a-tale-of:
F. Marion Crawford's 1885 tale of southern Italy opens with sailing directions across the Gulf of Salerno, past Licosa Point with its reefs and no light. A skipper of the old Leone dedicates the story to his middy, laddie, mate, and men. The coast, with pink and violet evening water, sets a romantic scene.

Children of the king, in Crawford's title sense, move through a world of sailors, friars, and seaside towns, where old barefoot friars stand beside heroines. The novel blends sea adventure with Italian local color. Readers who enjoy Crawford's romantic Italy will find the book sunny, vivid, and full of salt air.
15245-twenty-seven-years-in-canada-west-:
Major Strickland, edited by Agnes Strickland, tells of twenty-seven years in Canada West, from pioneer shanty to comfortable house and cleared farm. His preface argues that only a man who lived each grade of colonial life can describe it fairly. He filled many colonial posts, including commissioner roles.

Strickland traces backwoods toil, settlement growth, and the comforts of civilization won by his own exertions. A verse on naming new lands fronts the two-volume work, printed in London in 1853. Emigration historians will find the memoir detailed, personal, and full of early Canadian life.
15817-the-melting-of-molly:
A comic novel by Maria Thompson Daviess, in the American book form, drawn from Kentucky pages. Molly, a young Kentucky woman, keeps a diary of her campaign to grow thin. Her old love Al returns after eight years abroad, now attached to the legation at Saint James. Molly fears he will find her changed from the girl in the blue muslin dress.

Molly diets, walks, and worries, while family and friends tease her with drawling wit. The twenty-inch waist of her parting dress becomes her measure of hope. Daviess writes in Molly's own voice, frank and funny about vanity and love. The novel charms as a light romance: a girl learns that worth is not weighed, even as she chases the scale.
15818-the-melting-of-molly:
The British magazine version of Maria Thompson Daviess's The Melting of Molly, differing greatly from the American novel version. Where the novel runs in chapters, this version runs in leaves, opening with Leaf One, The Bachelor's-Buttons. Molly's diary voice leads again, frank, funny, and full of spring happiness. The magazine form suits short, bright instalments.

Molly, in a tingle of mind, vows to do her best and hold herself to no blame. Good feeling, from radiant joy to perfect bliss, fills her spring pages. Love, vanity, and the wish to grow thin still drive her story. Readers who know the novel will enjoy the contrast: the same heroine, told in a briefer, magazine key.
16299-henry-gally:
Henry Gally's Critical Essay on Characteristic-Writings, reprinted here, first introduced his 1725 translation of Theophrastus's Moral Characters. Gally lived from 1696 to 1769 in a moderately successful church career, becoming chaplain-in-ordinary to George II in 1735. His other works were sermons, tracts, and a treatise on Greek pronunciation, but his essay on character deserves attention for another reason.

It offers the first detailed, serious English discussion of a literary kind hugely popular in its day, the character sketch. Earlier writers like Overbury, who called character wit's descant on a plain song, and Brathwaite had only touched the form. Students of Augustan prose will find Gally's essay a landmark of early literary criticism.
16427-the-splendid-folly:
Margaret Pedler's 1921 novel follows Diana through a love that flares, breaks, and must be faced again. Chapter titles trace the arc: a verdict, a meeting, a brush with death, a singing voice, a contest of wills, the other woman, and the parting of the ways. Max Errington and Carlo Baroni stand at the heart of the tangle.

Pedler writes in the lush romantic style of her day, with scenes of country houses, music, and first nights. The pace is brisk, and the plot turns on choice and sacrifice rather than on mystery. For readers of popular romance between the wars, the book offers a full, emotional tale with a hard-won close.
16496-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-1-of-6-:
This second slice of Holinshed's Chronicles, volume one, opens with Raphael Holinshed's great history of England. It runs from its first inhabiting to its last conquest, newly digested into books and chapters by Abraham Fleming. Tables of particulars serve the description and the history, and a note to readers praises the order of the work.

The slice gives the chronicle's front matter and early books in Tudor spelling, with arguments prefixed to each chapter. As Shakespeare's chief history source, Holinshed needs no apology. Readers of early English prose will find this slice a direct taste of the chronicle's vast, orderly ambition.
16511-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-1-of-6-:
This fourth slice of Holinshed's Chronicles, book three, tells of Mulmucius, first king of Britain crowned with a golden crown. Son of Cloton, he beat the other dukes, took the whole monarchy, built a temple in London, then called Troinouant, and gave laws. Dates run by the year of the world, Rome's building, and Israel's deliverance.

The Tudor spelling is kept, with sidenotes from Matthew of Westminster and Geoffrey of Monmouth. As one slice of a vast chronicle, the volume gives early British legend in its original form. Readers of Shakespeare's sources will enjoy its quaint, confident history of kings before Rome.
16536-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-1-of-6-:
This slice of Holinshed's Chronicles, volume one, book four, carries the history of England into the Roman conquest. Plautius hunts the Britons through their lurking places, beats Cataratacus and Togodumnus, sons of Cynobellinus, and takes the chief city of Cymbeline's kingdom. Claudius earns the name Britannicus for the conquest.

The old spelling is kept, giving the text its Tudor flavor: Britains discomfited, sore wounded, and slaine fill the page. As one slice of a vast chronicle, the volume gives Shakespeare's source material in raw form. Readers of early English history will find it rough, vivid, and direct.
16555-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-1-of-6-:
This sixth slice of Holinshed's Chronicles, book five, follows Britain after Rome refused to govern it any longer. Constantinus, at the general suit of the Britons, takes up rule, is crowned king, fathers three sons, and is traitorously slain by a Pict. His eldest son Constantius, once a monk, is made king, while Duke Vortigern schemes for the crown.

Vortigern's crafty devices, deep dissimulation, and winning of hearts fill the argument. The Tudor spelling is kept, with sidenotes from Geoffrey of Monmouth. Readers of early British legend will find a vivid account of kings, treachery, and the long shadow of Rome.
16610-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-1-of-6-:
This seventh slice of Holinshed's Chronicles, book six, follows Ine, king of the West Saxons, as the whole monarchy falls into West Saxon hands. Ine grants peace to Kent for money, fights Gerent of the Britons and kings of Mercia and the South Saxons, gives up his royalty, goes on pilgrimage to Rome, and dies there. His Saxon laws and buildings get full note.

Queen Ethelburga's device to persuade Ine to forsake the world, Peter's pence, monk-kings, and a vision authorizing images fill the slice. The Tudor spelling is kept throughout. Readers of early English history will find a vivid, legend-rich account of Wessex rising to rule.
16617-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-1-of-6-:
This slice holds the seventh book of Holinshed's history of England, in old spelling, covering King Ethelred after Edward the Martyr. It tells of a weak reign, Dunstan's hard words to the king, the bishop of Rochester quarrel, and Danes landing in Kent to spoil town after town. Dunstan's life, his trance, his harp tale, and his dream of a rough bear fill much of the text.

The chronicle mixes kings, churchmen, and raids in the manner of Tudor history writing, with side notes and long chapter heads that sum up each turn. Readers get early England as Holinshed's age saw it: saints and sinners, wise counsel spurned, and a realm worn down by raids. The old spelling slows a first read but keeps the flavor of the first telling.
16669-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-1-of-6-:
This ninth and last slice of Holinshed's Chronicles, book eight, follows Edward III's path to the crown. Chosen king by general consent, Edward is attended home by ambassadors, crowned with William of Normandy beside him, and caught in Earl Goodwine's subtle ambition. The Danes are expelled, Goodwine's guilt over Alfred's death is weighed, and Edward marries Goodwine's daughter.

Queen Emma's hard usage, accusations, imprisonment, and strange purging fill the argument, with a lesson to mothers on equal love. The Tudor spelling is kept. Readers of English history will find a rich, legend-laden close to Holinshed's first volume.
16844-catalogue-of-the-william-loring-an:
Yale University Press issued this 1913 catalogue of the William Loring Andrews collection of early books in Yale's library, printed in an edition of three hundred copies. A conspectus lists manuscripts such as a life of Zeno, then printed books from a 1462 Mainz Latin Bible by Fust and Schoeffer, through Justinian and Isidore, onward.

The catalogue gives each book's author, title, place, printer, and date, with notes on type and state. It serves book lovers, librarians, and scholars who study early printing. The volume is a record of a great gift to Yale, and a useful tool for tracing the first century of print in Europe.
17570-religious-education-in-the-family:
Henry F. Cope, general secretary of the Religious Education Association, published this book with the University of Chicago Press in April 1915, with later impressions running to 1922. Chapters open with an interpretation of the family and the present state of family life, then turn to the permanent elements in family life and the religious place of the family.

Later chapters cover the meaning of religious education in the family, the child's religious ideas, directed activity, the home as a school, and the child's ideal life. Readers get a progressive-era guide to teaching faith at home, practical rather than doctrinal. Cope's book suits readers of religious education and of American family life a century ago.
17666-lucia-rudini-somewhere-in-italy:
Martha Trent wrote this story of Lucia Rudini, somewhere in Italy, published in New York in 1918 by Barse and Hopkins, with pictures by Charles L. Wrenn. A frontispiece shows Lucia telling a frightened Austrian soldier that he is her pet. Chapters run from Cellino and Maria, through before daybreak and lost, to a tool shed, Garibaldi performs, and the beggar.

The opening finds Lucia laughing at a sleepy boy in the grass, who dreams of killing a whole regiment of Austrians beside the soldiers up the hill. A surprise attack and a bridge follow later. Readers get a wartime Italian tale for young readers, full of courage, humour, and village life.
1808-the-log-of-the-jolly-polly:
Richard Harding Davis writes this comic log in the voice of a man to whom temptation always comes at the worst hour. He swears off drinking, and an ushers' dinner follows; he tries to grow rich, and only highbrow plans arrive. The Jolly Polly herself is a boat, and her log records a summer of sailing, friends, and small disasters.

Davis tells the story through a narrator who once lived at the New York end of a run in a flat, with no place for a boy to play but the street. The narrator found he could rent an old cottage across the water instead. The book is light, salty, and fond of its own rogues, and it reads as a holiday tale for readers who like the sea without the storms.
1857-initials-only:
Anna Katharine Green's Initials Only opens with poinsettias, a man known only by his initials, and a young woman named Miss Clarke in a red cloak. It follows a case in which George Brotherson's cold self-possession strikes another man like a blow. The letters, the partly lifted veil, and the strange doings for George all point to a crime hidden behind good manners.

Green tells the story from two strangers' points of view. The initials of the title become a puzzle in themselves: who is the man, and what does he hide. The novel is a compact, clever mystery, and it shows Green's gift for building suspense out of social detail rather than out of violence.
19180-scientific-american-volume-xxiv-no:
This March 18, 1871, issue of Scientific American offers practical information on art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and manufactures. Published weekly in New York by Munn and Company, it lists knots and splices, cold on iron and steel, oak graining, springs for rail carriages, and a portable writing case. Pictures mark the leading pieces.

A piece on oak graining praises hand work over machine pattern, urging soft contrasts and good taste in colour and combing. Other notes serve makers, builders, and engineers. Readers get a vivid weekly snapshot of American invention and craft in the years after the Civil War.
2074-the-civilisation-of-the-renaissance:
Jacob Burckhardt's classic study, in S. G. C. Middlemore's authorised translation, remains the founding account of the Italian Renaissance. Burckhardt treats the period not as a list of artworks but as a whole culture. Burckhardt first published the work in German in 1860, and it slowly won readers in English.

He writes of the state as a work of art, the growth of the individual, the revival of antiquity, and the new life of society and morals. Students still turn to this book first, and its broad view shaped how later writers saw the Renaissance. Middlemore's translation, from the third German edition, made the book accessible to students without German.
20929-little-novels-of-italy:
Giovanna kneels by green water most days, her hair waving like a flag, in Little Novels of Italy. Maurice Hewlett paints her as fit to plant in a castle. Calm lips and candid grey eyes mark his Italian heroines' grave grace.

Hewlett gathers short tales of old Italy, of love, pride, and sharp fate. Towns, courts, and peasants of a past age fill his rich scenes. His prose glows with colour, music, and a poet's touch. Readers who like tales steeped in place and passion will find Hewlett's Italy vivid, strange, and steeped in beauty of a bygone world.
21280-surgical-experiences-in-south-afri:
George Henry Makins was surgeon to St Thomas's Hospital in London and a consulting surgeon to the South African Field Force. He wrote this clinical study from the Boer War of 1899-1900. Published in London in 1901, it examines the nature and effects of wounds from small-calibre bullets. Makins dedicates it to the Royal Army Medical Corps men he served with.

His contents move from itinerary, surgical outfit, and the troops' general health into case after case of gunshot wounds he saw himself. Few cases beyond his own observation are quoted. The Mauser and Lee-Metford era of small, fast bullets changed wound surgery, and Makins records what that meant at the front.
21322-the-tale-of-betsy-butterfly:
Betsy Butterfly thinks her own name plain and wishes she had been called Violet, after a flower, in Arthur Scott Bailey's 1918 Tuck-Me-In Tale. Her red-and-brown mottled wings do not match her idea of beauty. Around her in Pleasant Valley live Mrs. Ladybug, Joseph Bumble, Dusty Moth, and Solomon Owl.

Johnnie Green's butterfly net opens the danger, and chapters follow mishaps, busybodies, a night watch, and a deep plot against her. Butterfly Bill and a friendly stranger complicate her summer. Bailey wrote these short animal tales for bedtime reading, each creature's habits turned into small comedy for children.
22525-john-lyly:
John Lyly studies the Elizabethan writer whose wit shaped English prose. Lyly's Euphues gave the language a fashion and a word: euphuism. The biographer hopes his solutions will serve Elizabethan students well.

His problems of Lyly's life may be faulty in detail, he admits. Still, presenting them from a single point of view helps. Several points demanded closer attention than they had yet received. The study gives that attention to Lyly's plays, prose, and court career. Lyly wrote for boy actors and royal audiences in his prime. His balanced, sparkling sentences influenced writers for a generation. Readers get a scholarly life of a once-famous, now half-forgotten stylist.
2311-travels-through-france-and-italy:
Tobias Smollett, the Scottish novelist, records a trip across France and Italy in letters full of complaint, observation, and splenetic humor. Travels through France and Italy covers Nice, Rome, and the road between, with Smollett grumbling about inns, weather, and foreigners while noting art, antiquities, and customs with a surgeon's eye. His bad temper is the book's entertainment.

The letters also document eighteenth century travel at its most uncomfortable: bad roads, fleas, and dubious doctors. Smollett's prejudices are on full display, and modern readers will take them as part of the period. The book remains a vivid, grumpy classic of travel writing.
23131-principle-and-practice-the-orphan-:
A plain promise opens Principle and Practice, the story of the orphan family. It is not a relation of uncommon circumstances, the narrator warns, of romantic adventures, poetical perplexities, or picturesque difficulties. No such beauties await the reader here, she warns. Her aim is a plain, unaffected account of how a family of young people worked to make themselves and each other happy and useful.

Harriet Martineau, to whom the tale is credited, wrote that promise into a story of orphaned siblings keeping a household by work and principle. Her didactic tales taught political economy and self-help to young readers. The anti-romance pledge is itself a small manifesto. Usefulness, in this book, is the adventure, and the family pursues it account-book in hand.
23381-the-thorogood-family:
R. M. Ballantyne shaped this family book in an odd, branching way. A first chapter sets out a young family. Later chapters follow the grown sons through varied exploits, with a schoolboy tale tucked in that owes nothing to the Thorogoods yet stands well on its own.

One son works as a missionary among the poor of London. The closing chapter adds a long tale of a third party. It ends with most of the family sailing off to the Rockies of North America. Ballantyne's gift for place and incident runs through it all, with two stories at times running side by side. Readers get a warm, rambling family saga rather than a single straight plot.
23523-adventures-in-toyland-what-the-mar:
Edith King Hall wrote this nineteen hundred toyland tale, with seventy pictures, of what the marionette told Molly. Dedicated to Dorothy and Doris, in memory of time spent in fairyland together, the book opens after the shutters are up, when toys wake and talk.

A rabbit and a mouse, Belinda, an officer and an elephant, and a little dancer each tell their tales. A hansom driver, proud Claribelle, and a grocer with a farthing doll each tell theirs, closing with a last performance. Hall writes with warmth and fancy, letting shop toys speak of their lives, hopes, and small griefs. Children will love the night world of the toy shop, while grown readers will enjoy the gentle humour and the tender view of playthings as friends.
23734-the-idler-magazine-vol-iii-may-189:
The Idler Magazine for May 1893 gathers stories, essays, and interviews for readers who liked their monthlies witty and well illustrated. Bret Harte leads with An Ingenue of the Sierras. A coach crosses Galloper's Ridge in darkness, lights out, while the Ramon Martinez gang of road agents waits to time its passage.

Other contents include Cynicus on the Modern Babylon, P. von Schönthan's Balder's Ball, Robert Barr's The Fear of It, and Sophie Wassilieff's Memoirs of a Female Nihilist. Raymond Blathwayt interviews the Lord Lieutenant at Dublin Castle in his Lions in Their Dens series. The issue is a lively sample of 1890s magazine culture, mixing adventure, satire, and society talk.
24118-we-didn-t-do-anything-wrong-hardly:
Roger Kuykendall wrote this comic science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction in May 1959, with pictures by Freas. A boy narrator insists, in his own tangled voice, that he and his friends only borrowed things for a little while and put almost everything back. With Skinny Thompson, the boy genius, they turn an old compression chamber lent by Mr. Fields into a spaceship with portholes, an air lock, and real bunks.

What they still need is a compressor. Skinny trades for one from Stinky Brinker. He fits the ship with radar made from a television set, antigravity, and an atomic power plant of his own invention. Kuykendall lets the joke build through the narrator's excuses. Readers get a funny boyhood tall tale of backyard spaceflight.
24652-diversions-in-sicily:
Henry Festing Jones wrote these diversions in Sicily, first published in 1909 and reissued at London in 1920. He dedicated the book to Enrico Pampalone. Enrico's father once sat with him on a terrace at Castellinaria, watching moonlight on the water. The father agreed the book might bear his son's name.

Jones's chapters follow a brigadier and a lottery, paladins and crusaders, and the shadowy troops of Sicilian legend, mixing travel, history, and fancy. His Sicily is a land of stories, where Orlando's knights still linger. Readers who love travel writing with a literary turn will enjoy these graceful, wandering diversions.
25023-the-biography-of-a-grizzly:
Ernest Thompson Seton's Biography of a Grizzly, copyrighted in 1899 and 1900, tells the life of Wahb, a grizzly of the Wind River Mountains and the Graybull country. Seton dedicates the book to days spent there, gathering chapters of Wahb's history from hunters, miners, and personal experience. Seton writes that no beast of the wild, heroic West surpassed Wahb in magnificence, dignity, and power, and that few individuals now remain about Yellowstone and other havens.

Wahb lived in the Meteetsee Valley, his character shaped by traps and wild rivals. None of these he now feared, though the odor of man and iron always warned him from the first. Love-seasons came and went leaving him alone in his prime as in his youth, and his habitual moroseness grew with his strength until any meeting him would call him dangerous. The book is natural history told as biography.
25045-chanticleer-a-thanksgiving-story-o:
Chanticleer, a Thanksgiving story of the Peabody family in its second edition from Boston and New York in 1850, asks a question. Should the glorious festival, celebrated all over the Union, be ushered in with no trumpet but governors' proclamations? The author offers a holiday book instead, in harmony with the anniversary, to please fellow countrymen, acquaint strangers with the custom, and awaken union and friendship at the genial season. Home characters fill the volume.

Chapters move from the landscape of the story and the arrival of the merchant and his people. Farmer folks from the west, the fortunes of the family, the children, a fashionable lady and her son, and the Thanksgiving sermon follow. A bedtime scene shows Peabody Junior settling his pillow and announcing sleep, while Master Robert pesters little Sam about Aunt Hannah's old green shade. The book is domestic Americana for the holiday table.
25820-the-silver-butterfly:
Mrs. Wilson Woodrow sets a love story in New York around a man come home from years abroad. Hayden has built rail lines in South America, Africa, and China, yet London and Paris only sharpen his sense of being alone. Back in his home city, he longs for old friends, known streets, and an easy life among kin who are not too near.

His path crosses a woman with a rich voice who longs to see his insect collection, above all a rare kind some say is gone for good, the Veiled Mariposa. Her plea stirs him in a way he half expects, and his hand shakes as he answers. From that meeting, the rare butterfly draws the two together, and the hunt for it shapes the course of the novel.
25855-stray-studies-from-england-and-ita:
John Richard Green, historian of England, gathers magazine papers on England and Italy in this 1876 volume, reworked from Macmillan's Magazine and the Saturday Review. Sunshine sketches open the book, with Cannes, the Cornice carnival, pirate towns of the Riviera, San Remo, and a winter retreat. Then come London pieces on Lambeth, the archbishops, and children by the sea.

Later studies turn to the Florence of Dante, Abbot Sampson of St. Edmunds, Venice and Tintoretto, early Oxford, the Angevin kings, and Capri with its Roman remains. A paper on a brother of the poor and one on the feast of the coral fishers round out the set. Green writes as a traveler with a historian's eye, fond of old stones and living towns alike.
26173-the-stephens-family:
Bascom Asbury Cecil Stephens wrote this genealogy at Los Angeles in 1892, and Alonzo Smith Bower printed it with a few additions at Lima, Ohio, in 1910. It traces the descendants of Joshua Stephens, born in 1733 in Berks County, Pennsylvania, to Welsh parents. Family tradition says his father, also Joshua, came from Wales with brothers David and Ebenezer.

Each person gets a number, with birth, marriage, and death dates, so a reader can trace a line back step by step. The book works through sons and daughters, spouses, and moves westward into Ohio and beyond. It serves as a plain record for family members hunting their own branch of the Stephens line.
26315-shakespeare-s-family:
Mrs. C. C. Stopes's Shakespeare's Family, issued in London and New York in 1901, records the ancestors and descendants of William Shakespeare, with an account of the Ardens. Part one traces the name, early localities, and the Shakespeare coat of arms, with the impalement of the Arden arms. Chapters follow the Ardens of Wilmecote, John Shakespeare, the poet himself, and his descendants.

Collateral lines, cousins, and contemporary Warwickshire Shakespeares fill later chapters, while part two treats the Park Hall and Longcroft Ardens and branches in other counties. Pictures show the Droeshout portrait, the birthplace, Anne Hathaway's cottage, and the poet's epitaph. The book serves readers tracing Shakespeare's kin and country roots.
26751-cully:
Jack Egan wrote this short science-fiction story, illustrated by Schelling. Its tagline says that by all the laws of nature Cully should have been dead. If he were alive, something waited for him to find. It opens beneath eighty feet of still, black water, hung like a death shroud, with Cully holding to sanity by his ragged breathing and the rhythmic pulsing of his heart.

After an hour of careful breathing, Cully moves, flexes an arm, and watches a mote of gold sand sift upward in the dark water. He discovers a yellow water-tight suit bearing an orange shield on black, a bubble helmet, air tanks, a radio, and a box. A humming of tiny voices fills his mind, his feet walk without his willing it, and a driving question repeats itself: Where is it? Something wonderful lies just beyond reach.
26978-salem-witchcraft-and-cotton-mather:
Charles W. Upham's 1869 reply defends his account of Salem witchcraft and Cotton Mather's part in it. Reprinted from the Historical Magazine and dedicated to its editor, Henry B. Dawson, the pamphlet answers critics who challenged Upham's reading of the trials.

Its sections examine how the Court of Oyer and Terminer was set up, who bore responsibility for it, and Mather's connection with the court, including spectral evidence and his letters. Upham writes as a Massachusetts historian determined to fix blame where the record puts it. He wrote from Salem on December 10, 1869, and the pamphlet was printed at Morrisania, New York.
28185-harper-s-young-people-november-4-1:
Harper's Young People for November 4, 1879, volume one, number one, is the first number of Harper's illustrated weekly for children, priced at four cents. Its lead story, The Brave Swiss Boy, opens near Meyringen, where Walter, a herdsman's son, watches a neighbour seize his family's cow. Toni Hirzel, drawn by C. S. Reinhart, fronts the issue.

Other pages offer stories, puzzles, and pictures for boys and girls, in the plain, moral style of the day. The weekly, at $1.50 a year, aimed to entertain and teach at once. This first number shows Harper's entering the children's market with care and high hopes.
28186-harper-s-young-people-november-11-:
Harper's Young People for November 11, 1879, volume one, number two, continues the children's weekly begun a week earlier. Its Swiss tale, The Brave Swiss Boy, part two, follows Walter up a zigzag path toward the Engelhorn peaks, past a glacier burnished by morning sun. He reaches a crag called the Warder of the Glacier. Rocks and loose stones tax his strength.

Other pages offer stories, pictures, and puzzles at four cents, with the weekly at $1.50 a year. The number keeps the plain, moral tone of the first issue. Young readers get mountain adventure, hard climbing, and a boy's courage in the Bernese Oberland.
28196-harper-s-young-people-november-18-:
Harper's Young People for November 18, 1879, volume one, number three, is an early number of Harper's children's weekly. Its lead tale, The Tournament, has schoolboys James and Henry joust with brooms and barrel-head shields for the favour of Mary, a schoolmate who shows neither boy a clear choice. James E. Kelly drew the tournament.

The number also continues The Brave Swiss Boy from the first issue, as Walter's family fight keeps its cow. Stories, pictures, and puzzles fill the rest at four cents. The issue shows Harper's weekly finding its voice: moral, lively, and aimed squarely at boys and girls.
28213-harper-s-young-people-november-25-:
Harper's Young People for November 25, 1879, volume one, number four, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its Swiss tale, The Brave Swiss Boy, part three, follows Walter and the chamois-hunters, as Mr. Seymour visits the cottage and praises Walter's recovery from vulture wounds. Liesli, the cow recovered through Seymour's kindness, stands outside.

The cover picture, The Day Before Thanksgiving, jokes about stuffing turkeys and selves in turn. Other stories and pictures fill the number. The issue keeps the weekly's mix of adventure, humour, and plain morals for boys and girls.
28246-harper-s-young-people-december-2-1:
Harper's Young People for December 2, 1879, volume one, number five, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its lead piece, The Twins, tells of young bears kept as household pets, playful and loving when young, and trained to ring bells, beat drums, and play dead. A Louisiana planter's cub Billy, raised with children, boxes and wrestles for guests.

The number warns that grown bears, with full teeth and claws, cannot be trusted, and that teasing often turns them wild. Other pages offer stories and pictures for boys and girls. The issue shows the weekly mixing animal lore with plain moral lessons.
28250-harper-s-young-people-december-9-1:
Harper's Young People for December 9, 1879, volume one, number six, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its lead tale, Twenty Miles an Hour, opens on January 6 in Russia, when the Neva is consecrated and soldiers parade. Ivan and Olga, kept in by their English governess for unruly lessons, watch sledges from warm rooms. An ice-hill picture fronts the number.

The children, muffled in furs in fancy, pace from porcelain stove to frosted windows, longing for the sights outside. Their story turns on a forbidden outing and a swift ride. The issue gives young readers a glimpse of Russian winter and a governess's rule.
28261-harper-s-young-people-december-16-:
Harper's Young People for December 16, 1879, volume one, number seven, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its tale, One Touch of Nature, by Mrs. W. J. Hays, follows Lily Douglas and her mother shopping for a Christmas charity fair. Lily, in a new velvet cloak and furs, curls into a carriage corner and wishes for snow.

Snow comes, first slow, then in earnest, as the brougham rolls through shops and streets. The story turns on a small kindness that bridges rich and poor at Christmas. The issue, with a picture of lovely children, keeps the weekly's gentle, moral tone.
28265-harper-s-young-people-december-23-:
Harper's Young People for December 23, 1879, volume one, number eight, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its Swiss tale, The Brave Swiss Boy, part seven, finds Walter waking in Paris to silk curtains, mirrors, carpets, and gilt pictures, after a long sleep. Mr. Seymour and a friend ask what Walter will do now that his money is back.

Walter answers that he will buckle his belt and return home that day, though Seymour urges a safer way to send the money. A Santa Claus at home picture fronts the number. The issue blends mountain adventure with Parisian wonder for young readers.
28275-harper-s-young-people-december-30-:
Harper's Young People for December 30, 1879, volume one, number nine, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its verse lead, A Coasting Song, follows children from a snow-thatched farmhouse into moonlight. They slide down a hill on sleds, swift as arrows, then trudge up again to a fire of oak and pine. C. Graham drew coasting on New Year's Eve.

The song welcomes the new year with bells, dancing, and joyous din over hill and dale, then leaves the hill silent as coasters go home. Other stories and pictures fill the number. The issue captures winter fun and new-year hope for young readers.
28300-harper-s-young-people-january-6-18:
Harper's Young People for January 6, 1880, volume one, number ten, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its natural-history piece, Squirrels and Wild-Cats, calls the squirrel the most graceful forest dweller, and explains the name Sciurus, from Greek words for shadow and tail. The chipmunk, the family's only burrower, digs yards-deep galleries for winter stores.

Other pages offer a family in danger, stories, and pictures for boys and girls. The weekly, at $1.50 a year, mixed animal lore with adventure and morals. The issue shows Harper's teaching nature through lively, plain prose.
28304-harper-s-young-people-january-13-1:
Harper's Young People for January 13, 1880, volume one, number eleven, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its lead serial, Jeanie Lowrie, the Young Immigrant, by F. E. Fryatt, opens at Castle Garden in New York, where eight-year-old Jeanie waits for her grandfather, Sandy Lowrie, who has gone into the city. Her luggage is small: treasures in a silk kerchief and Granny's umbrella.

Evening finds the great hall empty save for women and children by a stove, watched by officials. Jeanie, torn between pleasure and fright at the crowds, guards her charge. The issue offers a tender immigrant tale for young readers.
28313-harper-s-young-people-january-20-1:
Harper's Young People for January 20, 1880, volume one, number twelve, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its science talk, Our Own Star, has a professor teach May and Joe that the sun is our own star, ninety-two million miles away. It looks far brighter than other stars only because it is nearer. Earth, he says, is 7,920 miles through, no more than a plum beside the sun.

A verse on a cat waking a sleepy child opens the number. Other stories and pictures fill the rest. The issue shows Harper's teaching astronomy in plain dialogue, with questions from children and clear, homely comparisons.
28318-harper-s-young-people-january-27-1:
Harper's Young People for January 27, 1880, volume one, number thirteen, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its verse lead, The Dance in the Kitchen, has a tea-kettle sing a Scottish air and an Irish jig, while Bess dances with a courtesy and pussy cries bravo. Sol Eytinge drew the dance.

Other pages offer The Old Man of Montrose, whose long nose freezes stiff as an icicle, and stories and pictures for boys and girls. The number keeps the weekly's mix of verse, humour, and adventure. Young readers get a merry, musical issue for winter evenings.
28344-harper-s-young-people-february-3-1:
Harper's Young People for February 3, 1880, volume one, number fourteen, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its natural-history lead, The House-Sparrow, tells how the English sparrow reached America about twenty years earlier, first at Portland, Maine, then in New York parks. The birds came to fight the measuring-worm, which stripped city trees each spring.

Worms hung in webs from shade trees, leaving them bare by July, until sparrows ate them in numbers. A feeding-the-sparrows picture fronts the number. Other stories and pictures fill the rest. The issue shows Harper's teaching city nature through a pest's defeat.
28347-harper-s-young-people-february-10-:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, February 10, 1880, is the fifteenth number of the first volume of Harper and Brothers' illustrated weekly for children. It cost four cents. Its opening story, Old Father Time, has a professor explain to a sick girl and her friends how calendars came to be counted from the birth of Christ.

Like other numbers of the magazine, the issue pairs short stories and instructive pieces with pictures. The style is direct and meant for young readers. It offers a window on what American children were given to read in 1880: moral tales, general knowledge, and entertainment side by side in a single slim weekly.
28353-harper-s-young-people-february-17-:
Harper's Young People for February 17, 1880, volume one, number sixteen, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its history piece, General Prescott and the Yankee Boy, by Benson J. Lossing, tells how British General Prescott tyrannized Newport in 1777, knocking hats off with his cane and shouting, disperse, you rebels. Citizens despised him.

On a showery July night, Lieutenant-Colonel Barton and resolute men rowed from Providence, seized sentinels, burst Prescott's bedroom door, and carried him, undressed, across the bay to Warwick. A picture of a boy's wish fronts the number. The issue gives young readers a stirring Revolutionary tale.
28362-harper-s-young-people-february-24-:
Harper's Young People for February 24, 1880, volume one, number seventeen, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its adventure lead, Tracking a Buried River, offers 3,000 francs from the Scientific Association of Morlaix to anyone who traces the Larve river and finds whether it joins the sea underground. Two sailor boys, Pierre Lebon and Jacques Vaudry, take up the quest.

A year earlier, a man lowered with a lantern broke his light on a rock and had to be hauled up hurt. The boys, one Breton and one Guernsey-born, face the cleft with courage. A cold morning in a country school fronts the number. Young readers get a tale of science and daring.
28395-harper-s-young-people-march-2-1880:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, March 2, 1880, is the eighteenth number of the first volume of Harper and Brothers' illustrated weekly for children, priced at four cents. Its opening piece, A Hunting Adventure, tells of travel in the interior of Africa with a Portuguese ivory trader.

The narrator, recovering from fever, has become an expert shot, and hunts lion, elephant, and rhinoceros along a broad river lined with forest. Monkeys chatter in the branches, gazelles drink at the water, and a hippopotamus startles the canoes. The issue pairs such adventure with pictures and other short pieces, in the magazine's usual mix of excitement and instruction for young readers.
28404-harper-s-young-people-march-9-1880:
Harper's Young People for March 9, 1880, volume one, number nineteen, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its true story lead, Across the Ocean, or A Boy's First Voyage, by J. O. Davidson, opens as a tired, cold, hungry boy boards the steam-ship Arizona at New York, bound for China and the East by Suez. A firm mouth and bright eye mark his resolve.

The boy, with bag and bundle, pushes through a wharf house of shouting men and market crowds buying Christmas dinner. Davidson writes from life, with humour and warmth. The issue offers young readers a vivid start to a sailor boy's first voyage.
28410-harper-s-young-people-march-16-188:
Harper's Young People for March 16, 1880, volume one, number twenty, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its serial, Across the Ocean, chapter two, by J. O. Davidson, visits the forecastle of a steamer after dark, under a swinging lamp. Frank meets a grim dreamer, a scarred gaunt man, a handsome sinister face, and a shaggy giant with a tender heart.

A trim lad who knows Latin and Greek better than reefing lies beside them, his curly head recalling a fond mother. Frank meets with an accident in the picture. The issue continues a true sailor boy's voyage with colour and care.
28417-harper-s-young-people-march-23-188:
Harper's Young People for March 23, 1880, volume one, number twenty-one, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its verse lead, A Duet, by Margaret Eytinge, has two wee children sing a hymn in a doorway, one fair as morning, one dark as night, holding a hymn-book they cannot read. Arnak smiles, sure angels listen and see both children white.

Easter Flowers, by F. E. Fryatt, follows, as Miss Eleanor takes Nell and Harry to greenhouses to learn how florists bloom flowers out of season for Easter. Other stories and pictures fill the number. The issue offers spring verse and holiday learning for young readers.
28423-harper-s-young-people-march-30-188:
Harper's Young People for March 30, 1880, volume one, number twenty-two, is a children's weekly from Harper and Brothers, priced at four cents. Its verse lead, April-Fool, by Margaret Eytinge, introduces Harold Lord of Merrit Academy, a boy who never plays games, skates, swims, or debates, and who hates fighting, thunder, and tales of cruelty. Fair-haired, blue-eyed, and tall, Harold loves birds, flowers, verses, and fairy tales.

Harold, timid and credulous, believes in ghosts and shudders at war, while schoolmates plan April fool jokes. A delusion and a snare pictures the number. The issue offers young readers a gentle, comic portrait of a boy unlike his fellows.
28506-our-italy:
Charles Dudley Warner's Our Italy, published by Harper & Brothers in 1891, gives Southern California its nickname by likening it to Italy. The opening recalls a traveler descending an Alpine pass from snow into spring verdure, a surprise Warner finds matched on the Pacific coast. Santa Barbara, Riverside, Pasadena, and Los Angeles anchor the tour that follows.

Chapters treat climate, health, land prices, irrigation, and chances for laborers and small farmers. Fruit perils, cultivation southward, the desert, Laguna Pueblo, Yosemite, and the Grand Cañon all get their turn. Readers get a booster-era portrait of a new Mediterranean, sold as a land of agreeable homes.
28765-rafael-in-italy:
Etta Blaisdell McDonald and Julia Dalrymple wrote this 1910 school reader that teaches geography through a boy's travels in Italy. Young Rafael journeys from Venice, where he sees trained tops and Venetian beads, through Verona and Florence to Rome, Naples, and the buried city of Pompeii. Each chapter pairs a place with a scene a child can picture: grapes gathered in Tuscany, a run to Rome, a morning in the Colosseum.

The book belongs to the Little People Everywhere series, which taught world geography by following children in other lands. A vocabulary at the back gives the sounds of the Italian words used. It remains a charming window into how American schools once introduced children to Europe, with pictures of canals, ruins, and street life throughout.
28777-harper-s-young-people-april-6-1880:
The April 6, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly for children published by Harper and Brothers in New York. Volume one, number twenty-three, it sold for four cents a copy or a dollar and a half a year in advance. The issue opens with A Rabbit Day, a story by W. O. Stoddard about two boys, Jim and Charley, hunting rabbits with their dog Nap on crusted snow near the Adirondacks.

The number shows the magazine's mix of fiction and pictures for young readers, with a front illustration of the boys in the woods. Its careful notes on tracking, guns, and winter woods give a taste of outdoor life as children's magazines presented it in 1880. For readers of period children's writing, a single issue like this captures the format whole: short, lively, and made to be read aloud.
28778-harper-s-young-people-april-13-188:
The April 13, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number twenty-four, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, Nancy Hanson's Project by Howard Pyle, opens in Wilmington, Delaware, on the evening of the Battle of Brandywine. Country people drive into town in sledges and heavy carts for market day, selling butter, eggs, milk, and vegetables.

Friend William Stapler stops at Elizabeth Hanson's house in Shipley Street with eggs and butter, bringing news of cannon booming up by Chadd's Ford. Pyle, later famous for his illustrations, writes here in Quaker speech and careful period detail. The number shows the magazine at its best: a historical tale for children, told with pictures and a strong sense of place.
28790-harper-s-young-people-april-20-188:
The April 20, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number twenty-five, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, Sim Vedder's Kite by W. O. Stoddard, opens with the kite fever visiting Hagarstown every year and catching all the boys over five. This year three kites fly at once over the main street, while Squire Jones's pony bolts into a canter.

The squire bans more dangerous nonsense in the streets, so the boys move to Dr. Gay's pasture with eight kites. Then Sim Vedder, the thin hired man with the twisted nose, arrives carrying an enormous kite. The number shows the magazine's gift for small-town boy life, told with humor and a keen eye for how a whole village joins a craze.
28833-harper-s-young-people-april-27-188:
The April 27, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number twenty-six, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its serial Across the Ocean, by J. O. Davidson, reaches chapter eight, A White Squall. Young Frank, on his first voyage, learns the Straits of Gibraltar measure thirteen miles across, not as narrow as the East River as he had thought.

The chapter celebrates the Mediterranean, its sunny skies and sparkling waters, while warning that the glassy sea can turn stormy without notice. Spanish sailors in red caps and blue shirts cruise in lateen-rigged fruit boats, and an old sailor predicts trouble ahead. The number shows the magazine's true travel storytelling, with a front picture of Spanish sailors in a storm.
28881-harper-s-young-people-may-4-1880-a:
The May 4, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number twenty-seven, sold for four cents a copy from Harper and Brothers in New York. The issue opens with Rob's Navy, a story by W. O. Stoddard. It tells of twelve-year-old Rob Drake of Staten Island, who cannot make his model ship float upright. With Larry McGee, the hired man, he has whittled and worked on it for a week, yet every launch ends bottom up.

The story's charm lies in Rob's sure belief that he knows all about ships. He lives across the bay from New York's wharves and ferries, yet faces the plain fact of a top-heavy toy. The number shows the magazine's blend of fiction and pictures for children, with an illustration of old one-legged sailor Jack Peabody. It captures the weekly's voice whole: lively, instructive, and close to a child's world.
28882-harper-s-young-people-may-11-1880-:
The May 11, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number twenty-eight, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading piece, Hunting in Arctic Regions, explains that the Innuit hunter spends most time on the seal, which gives him food, fuel, and clothing. Captain Hall is quoted: the seal means to the Innuit all that flocks, grain fields, forests, and coal mines mean to others.

The article tells how the bear, Ninoo, taught men to hunt the seal, Nutchook, whose naps last about ten seconds at a time. A short poem, Why, opens the number, with a young bird asking its mother why it must learn to sing and fly. The number shows the magazine teaching natural history and far places, with a front picture of hunting in Arctic regions.
28895-harper-s-young-people-may-18-1880-:
The May 18, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number twenty-nine, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its serial Across the Ocean, by J. O. Davidson, reaches chapter eleven, Among the Coolies. The scene is Singapore at Chinese New Year, blazing with lanterns, banners, fireworks, and cannon.

Young Frank, helping load the ship Arizona, watches gangs of Malay and Chinese laborers carry tin blocks, rice sacks, opium chests, and pepper bags aboard. A Parsee merchant in a long white robe checks each man's name. The number shows the magazine's mix of true travel story and pictures, with a front illustration of loading at Singapore. It captures a boy's first voyage in vivid period detail.
28923-harper-s-young-people-may-25-1880-:
The May 25, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its opening poem, Memorial Flowers by M. M., calls children to gather blue violets, red columbines, and white star flowers at dawn, to scatter over soldiers' mounds in the red, white, and blue they loved. A front picture shows a mother's anxieties, with water everywhere.

A second piece, How Jonathan Bewitched the Chickens by Mary Hicks, opens with twenty boys tumbling out of a Boston schoolhouse, free because the master is called a witch. The boys wear long coats, small clothes, and buckled shoes, nearly two centuries before the reader's day. The number mixes holiday verse with colonial humor, in the magazine's varied style.
28975-harper-s-young-people-june-1-1880-:
The June 1, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-one, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, The Moral Pirates by W. L. Alden, opens with Mr. Wilson troubled about his boy Harry, idle from July to mid-September and reading wretched pirate stories. Uncle John answers that all boys like pirate tales, and offers to find Harry a summer task.

Uncle John recalls his own boyhood wish to be a pirate or a stage-driver, and his dream of being a moral and benevolent pirate, with a schooner of his own. The number shows the magazine turning a parent's worry into adventure, with a front picture of the moral pirates examining their craft. Readers get a charming start to a summer serial about boys playing pirate without the murder and robbery.
28984-harper-s-young-people-june-8-1880-:
The June 8, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-two, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its serial The Moral Pirates, by W. L. Alden, reaches chapter two, as Uncle John approves the captain and crew of the Whitewing and the boys lay in stores. Each boy takes a fishing line and hooks, and Harry and Tom take poles.

The boat carries a coffee pot, tin pans, pails, blankets, a hatchet, cordage, and a lantern, with coffee, sugar, Indian meal, crackers, canned soup and meats, peaches, and a cold boiled ham. The number shows the magazine's love of practical detail, listing every item a boy crew would need. Readers get a charming chapter of summer boating, told with care for gear and grub.
29002-harper-s-young-people-june-15-1880:
The June 15, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-three, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, Charley's Balloon Voyage by Frank H. Taylor, opens with Harry running down the road crying that a balloon is coming. Charley is nowhere to be found, having wandered to his favorite rock by the brook for a good cry.

Charley had dreamed for two weeks of a circus poster showing leaping horses, trick mules, clowns, and a great balloon rising over a crowd. His mother promised to take him, but she fell sick before the show, and no one else could go. The number captures a child's disappointment with warmth, and sets up a balloon adventure to follow. Readers get a period children's story, lively and tender at once.
29009-harper-s-young-people-june-22-1880:
The June 22, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-four, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its opening poem, Baby, Bee, and Butterfly by Mary D. Brine, pictures a baby boy under the summer sky, watching sunbeams tumble in the clover while bees work all day. The verse wishes him wisdom enough to spell baby with a great big B.

A second piece, An American Soldier of Fortune by M. Lockwood, begins the life of William Eaton, born February 23, 1764, son of a Woodstock farmer with thirteen children. The number shows the magazine's mix of verse for small children and history for older ones, with a front picture of recess at the academy. Readers get a pleasant, varied weekly, made for family reading.
29016-harper-s-young-people-june-29-1880:
The June 29, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-five, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its serial The Moral Pirates, by W. L. Alden, reaches chapter five in a terrific storm. Wind sweeps down the river, rain falls harder than the boys have ever seen, and lightning and thunder frighten them in their tent.

Joe boasts too soon that they are dry as in a house, for water runs in under the tent and the boys must stand holding their blankets. Worse, the tent pins, only four used, cannot hold in loosened earth, and the tent blows down. A front picture shows a soup explosion. Readers get a comic storm chapter, full of boyish trouble and good humor.
29026-harper-s-young-people-july-6-1880-:
The July 6, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-six, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, The Mohawk Bowmen by J. O. Davidson, opens with Harry asking Foster what he is doing, shooting with a bow and arrows. Foster, taught by Stuart, hits a collar box on a grassy bank again and again, to Harry's wonder and envy.

Stuart owns a bow taller than its owner, over six feet long, and killed a deer with an arrow in the mountains a week before. He proposes an archery club, where the boys will make their own bows and arrows as Indians do, camp near the Glen, and hunt on Saturdays. A front picture shows Mohawk bowmen in the woods. Readers get a boys' archery adventure, full of craft and outdoor fun.
29034-harper-s-young-people-july-13-1880:
The July 13, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-seven, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, A Crabbing Adventure by Matthew White Jr., follows George and Bert Fielden, whose father has died and whose family finances are often discussed. The boys dream of selling soft crabs at sixty to seventy-five cents a dozen, to spare their mother sewing.

Mrs. Fielden fears the river will swallow them, but at last consents, and Captain Sam sells them a second-hand boat at a trifling price. A front picture, drawn by C. S. Reinhart, shows setting the crab net. The number captures a family's need and two boys' enterprise, in the magazine's lively, practical style for young readers.
29043-harper-s-young-people-july-20-1880:
The July 20, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-eight, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, The Biggest Blackberry Picker by W. O. Stoddard, follows Dot Calliper on a mountainside berrying party. Dot fills her little pail. Dot, too small and stout to climb further, stays behind beneath a great chestnut tree, minding the milk pails while the others go on.

The pails already hold great, plump berries, the best anyone ever saw in those mountains. A fire three years before let the bushes take the country. Dot sits alone, half sorry the near berries are picked, while Jessie, Betsy, and Molly pick nearby. A front picture shows a poor, dead bear. Readers get a gentle summer story of a small child's patience.
29050-harper-s-young-people-july-27-1880:
The July 27, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number thirty-nine, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, Poddie and Dick at the Free Bath by Uncle Frank, opens with Poddie Monell stamping his foot at the South Ferry gate, sure Uncle Fritz will never come. Dick spots him beyond the Elevated, and the gentleman, giving a hand to each, leads them to the Battery's walks.

Dick asks which free bath they will visit and what they are like, hoping for hanging rings, a flying trapeze, and diving places like the Central Park bath. His uncle explains the Battery bath has space, ropes, diving places, and depth, and lists four East River baths and three on the North River. A front picture, drawn by A. D. Shults, shows a free swimming bath. Readers get a pleasant New York summer story for boys.
29066-harper-s-young-people-august-3-188:
The August 3, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number forty, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its serial The Moral Pirates, by W. L. Alden, reaches chapter ten, as the boys sleep past sunrise, row to a steamboat landing, and breakfast at a hotel. The waiters marvel at the appetites of four sunburned boys, and the landlord likely loses money that morning.

Harry finds a waterproof India rubber bag from the Department at the express office, letters from home at the post office, and a ten-dollar postal order from Uncle John. Stores bought at Albany refill the low provisions, and by ten o'clock the Whitewing is afloat again toward Troy and the canal. A front picture, drawn by A. B. Frost, shows going through the lock.
29087-harper-s-young-people-august-10-18:
Dated August 10, 1880, this number 41 issue of Harper's Young People opens with a new chapter of Alden's serial The Moral Pirates. Tom and his friends, camped out along a canal, argue over what day of the week it is after six nights sleeping outdoors. They settle on Sunday and give up the idea of moving on.

Elsewhere in the issue, readers find easy botany notes on August wild flowers. David Ker tells of a boy emigrant in Russia. Benson Lossing adds a chapter of his history of the American navy. Short pieces cover a rainy-day game and a greedy little mouse. Readers get a typical week of the magazine: serial adventure, nature, history, and small tales side by side.
29099-harper-s-young-people-august-17-18:
The August 17, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number forty-two, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its historical piece, Old Times in the Colonies by Charles Carleton Coffin, tells of John Kerzar, Hannah Dustin, and the Indians. In August 1692, Kerzar mows his meadow by the Merrimac with his gun leaned against a tree, when an Indian creeps through tall grass to seize it.

Kerzar, brave and quick, rushes the Indian with uplifted scythe and a trumpet yell, and the man falls dead. The piece then turns to Haverhill, a frontier settlement often attacked, and to Thomas Dustin's family of eight children. A front picture, drawn by Howard Pyle, shows the escape of Hannah Dustin. Readers get colonial history told as adventure for children.
29108-harper-s-young-people-august-24-18:
The August 24, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number forty-three, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading piece, Some Queer Racing-Craft, describes two kinds of swift sailboats common near New York and rare elsewhere, built expressly for speed and used almost entirely for racing. The boats are light of draught, cabinless, and oversparred, carrying sails far larger than their size warrants.

Most are sloop-rigged, with main booms so long that the main sheet is trimmed from a platform overhanging the stern. Crews of twelve to twenty men shift sandbags as ballast, and thousands of dollars are wagered on races. Famous boats named include the Susie S., Nettle, Martha M., and Dare-Devil. Readers get a lively lesson in yacht racing for children.
29115-harper-s-young-people-august-31-18:
The August 31, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number forty-four, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, Claudine's Doves by Mrs. E. W. Latimer, opens with a slender, sweet girl of about fifteen walking in the Bois de Boulogne beside her mother. A friend calls her the heroine of a very pretty story, set eight years earlier in a flat in the Rue de Rivoli.

Claudine's windows looked over the Tuileries gardens, chestnut trees, fountains, the Seine, and the Place de la Concorde, and every procession passed below. Her parents, of good birth and schooling, were not rich, but no little girl overlooking the Rue de Rivoli would trade her home. Readers get a charming Paris story for children, told with a traveler's eye.
29134-harper-s-young-people-september-7-:
The September 7, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number forty-five, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, Wally, the Wreck-Boy by Frank H. Taylor, follows Wallace, a lighthouse keeper's son on the northern coast. Wally, about twelve, seldom finds a playmate, but Elsie Burton, a bright-eyed girl from a cottage two miles down the beach, rides over on a small donkey to see his museum.

Wally proudly shows curious shells, seaweed, sharks' teeth, fish bones, and full-rigged ships whittled on winter nights, while Elsie shows her sketchbook pictures. A life-saving station stands near the lighthouse, and a front picture shows light-house sketches. Readers get a gentle seaside story of a lonely boy, a kind girl, and the treasures of the shore.
29174-harper-s-young-people-october-5-18:
Number 49 of Harper's Young People, dated October 5, 1880, leads with David Ker's Canadian story Hanging by a Thread. Tom Lockyer and his two cousins spend a summer morning in the woods, climbing trees, tearing through briers, and scrambling over rocks, until a perilous escape tests them. An illustration shows Fred's perilous escape.

The issue also offers a steam-engine made from a tin can, another chapter of John Habberton's Who Was Paul Grayson, and Charles Carleton Coffin's Old Times in the Colonies. John Stark and the Indians, Lil's Fun, and the closing chapter of Conny's story complete the number. Readers get a busy weekly for children, mixing adventure, science projects, and history.
29180-harper-s-young-people-october-12-1:
Number 50 of Harper's Young People, dated October 12, 1880, leads with Elinor Vey's story Coachy, about an old yellowish-brown hen scratching in a garden walk. The narrator watches the tousled bird peck and croon, then tosses a small stone her way, setting off the tale's mishap.

The rest of the issue keeps up the variety. It carries another chapter of John Habberton's Who Was Paul Grayson, Sara Keables Hunt on baptizing Coptic babies, and a history of Sandy Hook. Short items include a storm-petrel, a mishap, corn-stalk cattle, and a letter from Bessie Maynard to her doll. Readers get a full weekly mix for children, from farmyard humor to faraway customs.
29200-harper-s-young-people-october-19-1:
Number 51 of Harper's Young People, dated October 19, 1880, leads with William Stoddard's Rabbits to Find. Tad Murray, late with his cows, blames old Ben the cow-dog, who tears corn shocks to pieces chasing rabbits hidden inside them. The cornfield, Tad says, is just alive with rabbits.

The issue also carries another chapter of John Habberton's Who Was Paul Grayson, a piece on parasol ants and foraging ants, and Kate Greenaway's The Months. Sumac hunting, old times in the colonies, the battle of the rangers, and a visit to Viareggio, Italy, complete the number. Readers get a lively weekly for children, mixing farm humor, nature, and travel.
29238-harper-s-young-people-october-26-1:
Number 52 of Harper's Young People, dated October 26, 1880, leads with Frank Taylor's Work's a Mint, or Wilbert Fairlaw's Notion. Judge Barton stops a boy perched on a fence and questions him: his name is Wilbert Fairlaw, he does not go to school, and he tends his mother's cows and fetches wood. The judge tells him to find something that wants fixing and go at it.

The issue also offers Posy Parker's Halloween, another chapter of John Habberton's Who Was Paul Grayson, and William Stoddard's King Jack-o'-Lantern. The Sons of the Brave and embroidery for girls complete the number. Readers get a late-October weekly for children, seasonal and varied, closing the magazine's first volume.
29249-harper-s-young-people-1880-index-a:
Harper and Brothers published this index to Harper's Young People for 1880, the magazine's first year. The volume does not reprint stories; it guides readers to them. Its index to illustrations lists entries page by page, from Across the Ocean through the story of the American navy, the Moral Pirates, and Paul Grayson.

Entries cover Coney Island sketches, Juan Fernandez, lighthouse sketches, maple sugar, old times in the colonies, and the history of Photogen and Nycteris. A reader hunting a picture or a serial can find its place at once. Readers today get a map of a whole year of children's reading, useful for tracking a favorite serial or illustration through the weekly numbers.
29307-north-american-medical-and-surgica:
Hugh L. Hodge, Charles D. Meigs, Franklin Bache, Benjamin H. Coates, and Rene La Roche conducted this number of the North American Medical and Surgical Journal, volume two, number three, published in Philadelphia in July 1826 by J. Dobson. The journal's motto promises not more learned doctrine, but better imbued doctrine. Its editors deposited the title in March 1826.

Contents divide into original communications, analytical reviews, and a quarterly summary of medical and surgical intelligence. The summary runs through anatomy, physiology, pathology, therapeutics and materia medica, surgery, and midwifery. Readers get a window into early American medicine, when Philadelphia physicians surveyed European and American practice for a growing profession.
29512-olive-in-italy:
Moray Dalton's Olive in Italy, printed in London in 1909 by T. Fisher Unwin, follows Olive Agar through three books: Siena, Florence, and Rome. It opens in Siena, where a landlady's daughter tells Gwen that Olive is about to say she cannot pay her bill. Olive loves Italy and Italian cooking, and she hates boiled potatoes, a small, telling detail of her taste.

Dalton writes a novel of travel, money, and feeling, as Olive moves through Italian cities with wit and worry. The epigraph speaks of a cup of red wine poured out, whose dregs the ungodly shall drink. Readers of Edwardian travel fiction will enjoy a charming, observant tale of an Englishwoman abroad.
29725-the-fairchild-family:
Mrs. Sherwood wrote The Fairchild Family, edited with an introduction by Mary E. Palgrave and pictures by Florence M. Rudland, printed in New York by Frederick A. Stokes Company. Its history of Lucy, Emily, and Henry Fairchild began in 1818, nearly a century before this edition. A picture shows Mr. and Mrs. Fairchild with their three children.

Palgrave notes that Lucy, Emily, and Henry led lives we should call dull nowadays, yet the children themselves were anything but dull. Chapters follow the birthday walk, stories of apples, envy, ambition, and an unhappy day. Young readers and students of children's literature will find a classic of moral tales for the nursery.
29890-the-doctor-s-family:
